title: The five qualifications of the President (Art. VII, Sec. 2)
items: A natural-born citizen of the Philippines
A registered voter
Able to read and write
At least forty years of age on the day of the election
A resident of the Philippines for at least ten years immediately preceding the election
hook: Born here, listed, literate, forty, ten years home. Statute adds the ineligibilities (Buenafe).

title: The term rules (Art. VII, Sec. 4)
ask: State the rules on the term of the President and the Vice-President.
items: Elected by direct vote of the people for six years
The term begins at noon on June 30 after the election and ends at noon of the same date six years later
The President is not eligible for any reelection
A successor who served more than four years may never be elected President
The Vice-President may not serve more than two successive terms
Voluntary renunciation does not interrupt the continuity of service
The regular election is on the second Monday of May, unless the law provides otherwise
The Supreme Court en banc is the sole judge of contests on the election, returns and qualifications of the President and VP
hook: Six years from noon of June 30; no second term for the elected; four years for the successor; two for the VP.

title: Stopping an ineligible candidate: Sec. 78 or disqualification (Buenafe)
ask: How do a petition to cancel a COC and a petition for disqualification differ?
items: Sec. 78 ground: a deliberate false material representation in the COC (eligibility, age, citizenship, residence)
Disqualification ground: Secs. 12 and 68 of the OEC (final sentence over 18 months, moral turpitude, insanity, election offenses)
Sec. 78 period: within five days after the last day for filing COCs, not later than 25 days from the filing of the COC
Disqualification period: after the last day for filing COCs, not later than proclamation
Cancelled COC: the person was never a candidate and cannot be substituted
Disqualified: stops being a candidate; may be substituted if the COC was valid
Overlap: a disqualification ground may support Sec. 78 when it makes the sworn claim of eligibility false
hook: Lie in the COC: cancel (never a candidate). Ground in the law: disqualify (may be substituted).

title: When the PET takes over (Buenafe)
ask: When does the Presidential Electoral Tribunal acquire jurisdiction, and what may be filed there?
items: A petition is filed with the PET
Against a candidate who has been validly proclaimed
Who has taken the oath
And who has assumed office (the term starts at noon of June 30)
Election protest: within 30 days of proclamation, by the second or third placer
Quo warranto: within 10 days of proclamation, by any voter, on ineligibility or disloyalty
Before that, Rule 64/65 petitions from the COMELEC stay with the Court; and the PET is the Court itself
src: Buenafe v. COMELEC (2022); Art. VII, Sec. 4
hook: Proclaimed, sworn, seated: then the PET.

title: The President’s salary and privileges (Art. VII, Sec. 6)
ask: State the rules on the President’s residence and compensation.
items: An official residence
Salaries of the President and VP are determined by law
They may not be decreased during the tenure
An increase takes effect only after the term of the incumbent during which it was approved
No other emolument during the tenure, from the Government or any other source
So the salary is the whole lawful income from office; wealth manifestly out of proportion is presumed ill-gotten (RA 1379, Sec. 2)
src: Art. VII, Sec. 6; Republic v. Sandiganbayan (2003)
hook: One salary, no extras; no cut now, no raise till the next term.

title: Why the Swiss deposits were forfeited (2003)
ask: Why did the Court forfeit the Marcos Swiss deposits?
items: The Marcoses were public officers (admitted)
They owned the deposits: admissions in the answer, the settlement agreements, Marcos Jr.’s testimony, Imelda’s 90% claim
US$356 million was manifestly out of proportion to their salaries of about US$304,000
Their salaries were their only lawful income: no statements of assets, and the President could receive no other emolument
The presumption under RA 1379 arose and the burden shifted to them; they did not prove lawful acquisition
Their denials were sham, so summary judgment was proper
Laches and estoppel do not run against the State
hook: Officer, ownership, out of proportion: the burden shifts.

title: Who becomes or acts as President
ask: Give the rule of succession for each situation.
items: President-elect fails to qualify: the VP-elect acts as President until he qualifies (Sec. 7)
No President chosen: the VP-elect acts as President until one is chosen and qualified (Sec. 7)
President-elect dies or is permanently disabled at the beginning of the term: the VP-elect becomes President (Sec. 7)
Neither chosen or qualified, or both dead or disabled: the Senate President, or the Speaker, acts as President (Sec. 7)
President dies, is permanently disabled, removed or resigns: the VP becomes President for the unexpired term (Sec. 8)
Both offices vacant during the term: the Senate President, or the Speaker, acts as President; Congress calls a special election (Secs. 8 and 10)
VP office vacant: the President nominates a Member of Congress, confirmed by a majority of all the Members of both Houses voting separately (Sec. 9)
Temporary inability: the VP acts as President on a written declaration (Sec. 11)
hook: Vacancy: the VP becomes. Failure to qualify or inability: someone only acts.

title: Estrada resigned: the acts the Court counted
ask: What acts showed that Estrada resigned on January 20, 2001?
items: He proposed a snap election in which he would not run
He did not object to a “dignified exit or resignation”
He negotiated only the terms of his exit: a transition period, his family’s security, the second envelope
“Pagod na pagod na ako. Ayoko na”: words of resignation
Both sides’ draft agreements were premised on his resignation
His farewell statement acknowledged Arroyo’s oath and left the Palace “for the sake of peace”
He spoke of his presidency in the past tense and called for reconciliation, without saying he would return
hook: Before, during, after: the totality test.

title: What Art. VII, Sec. 13 forbids the President’s official family
ask: What does Sec. 13 prohibit, and to whom?
items: Covered: the President, VP, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants
No other office or employment, public or private, during the tenure, unless the Constitution provides otherwise
No practice of any other profession
No participation in any business
No financial interest in any contract, franchise or special privilege granted by the Government or a GOCC
Strictly avoid conflict of interest

The President’s spouse and relatives within the fourth civil degree may not be appointed to the Constitutional Commissions, the Ombudsman, or as Secretaries, Undersecretaries, or heads of bureaus, offices or GOCCs
hook: No second office, profession, business or stake; and no relatives in the top posts.

title: The exceptions to Sec. 13 (Civil Liberties Union)
ask: When may a member of the President’s official family hold another post?
items: The VP as a Cabinet member (Art. VII, Sec. 3), without confirmation
The VP acting as President (Art. VII, Sec. 7)
The Secretary of Justice as ex officio member of the JBC (Art. VIII, Sec. 8(1))
An ex officio post provided by law
And required, not merely allowed, by the primary functions of the office
And held without additional compensation: no per diem, honorarium or allowance by any name
Alternates and representatives cannot be paid either (Cruz; NAC v. COA)
src: Civil Liberties Union (1991); Cruz v. COA (2001); NAC v. COA (2004)

title: Where the Truth Commission’s power came from (Biraogo)
ask: Which sources did the Court reject and accept for the President’s power to create the Truth Commission?
items: Not the power to reorganize (Administrative Code, Book III, Sec. 31): it alters existing offices, it does not create them
Not the power of control: it reviews subordinates’ acts; it is different from creating offices
Not PD 1416: a transitional delegation, functus officio when Congress convened
Yes, the faithful-execution clause (Art. VII, Sec. 17): the inherent power to investigate and create ad hoc bodies
Funding from existing OP appropriations is an allotment, not an appropriation
Fact-finding is not adjudication: it does not supplant the Ombudsman or the DOJ
But EO 1 violated equal protection by singling out the previous administration
hook: Not reorganize, not control, not PD 1416: faithful execution. Then equal protection.

title: A valid reorganization of the Executive (Banda)
ask: What makes a presidential reorganization valid?
items: The office is in the Executive: not the Judiciary, Congress or a constitutional body
It alters an existing structure (abolish, merge, transfer, modify functions); creating a new office is not reorganization
A statutory basis: Administrative Code, Book III, Secs. 20 and 31, and the GAAs, read with the power of control
Good faith: for economy or efficiency (Dario v. Mison)
Bad faith (a change of names, false economy, a purge) voids it; whoever alleges it must prove it
The power may be delegated to the Secretary as alter ego (DENR v. DENR Region 12)
src: Banda v. Ermita (2010); Biraogo (2010); DENR v. DENR Region 12 (2003)

title: Control versus supervision
ask: Define control and supervision, and say whom each covers.
items: Control: alter, modify, nullify or set aside a subordinate’s act and substitute one’s judgment (Mondano v. Silvosa)
Control covers all executive departments, bureaus and offices (Art. VII, Sec. 17), every employee, and may be exercised motu proprio
Control is self-executing and cannot be withdrawn by Congress (NEA v. COA)
Qualified political agency: the Secretaries’ acts are presumptively the President’s unless disapproved
Supervision: see that the rules are followed; may not lay down, modify or replace them (Drilon v. Lim)
Supervision covers local governments and autonomous regions (Art. X, Secs. 4 and 16)
Supervision allows investigation and discipline as the law provides, but not withholding LGU powers or funds (Pimentel v. Aguirre)
src: Art. VII, Sec. 17; Art. X, Secs. 4 and 16

title: When the President may adjust the LGUs’ share (LGC Sec. 284)
ask: What must concur before the President may reduce the internal revenue allotment?
items: An unmanaged public sector deficit of the national government
Consultation with the Senate President and the Speaker
Consultation with the presidents of the leagues of local governments
The recommendation of the Secretaries of Finance, the Interior and Local Government, and Budget
The allotment may never go below 30% of the national internal revenue of the third preceding fiscal year
Otherwise the share is released automatically, with no lien or holdback, even temporarily (Art. X, Sec. 6; LGC Sec. 286)
hook: Deficit, consult, recommend, 30% floor; else no holdback.
